definition: Allocation of certain intangible or lease-asset cost over time.
A controlled economic resource expected to provide future benefit.
Snapshot of assets, liabilities, and shareholders' equity at a date.
Cash spent to acquire or build long-lived productive assets.
Recording spending as an asset rather than an immediate expense.
Direct or allocated cost of delivering the product or service sold.
Systematic allocation of a tangible asset's recorded cost over useful life.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization; not free cash flow.
Operating cash flow less defined capital investment; company definitions vary.
Gross profit divided by revenue.
Write-down when an asset's carrying value is not recoverable under the accounting test.
Accounting profit after operating costs, interest, taxes, and other items.
Cash generated or consumed by normal operations, including working-capital changes.
Operating income divided by revenue.
Period costs of operating the business, including many recurring costs and R&D.
Property, plant, and equipment: tangible long-lived operating assets.
Amount earned from selling goods or services before expenses.
Estimated period over which an asset provides accounting benefit.
Processor specialized for parallel numerical workloads such as AI.
Application-specific integrated circuit designed for a narrower workload.
Processing multiple requests together to improve hardware utilization.
Saved model state used to resume training or deploy a version.
Hardware, memory, networks, energy, software, and operations used to execute numerical work.
Amount of tokenized information a model can attend to in a request.
One floating-point arithmetic operation.
Floating-point operations per second at a stated numerical precision.
Computation that maps inputs through a model to outputs.
Highly parallel processor originally developed for graphics and widely used for AI.
Running a trained model to produce outputs.
Time required for a request or operation to complete.
Theoretical maximum under specified ideal conditions.
Methods after pre-training that shape behavior and task performance.
Large-scale parameter learning from broad datasets.
Reinforcement learning: learning from rewards or evaluated outcomes.
Work completed per unit of time.
A unit of text or code consumed or generated by a model.
Google's tensor processing unit family of AI accelerators.
Updating model parameters using data and optimization.
Fraction of available resource capacity doing productive work.
Third-party facility in which customers place or reserve IT equipment/capacity.
Servers, accelerators, memory, networking, storage, and related equipment.
Milestone at which a site or equipment receives usable electrical power.
One billion watts; a power rate, not an energy quantity.
One million watts; common data-center capacity unit.
One megawatt used or generated for one hour; an energy quantity.
Power purchase agreement governing electricity supply and pricing.
Total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy.
Connecting many servers or racks across a larger distributed cluster.
Tightly coupling accelerators with very high-bandwidth low-latency links.
One billion kilowatt-hours; large annual energy unit.
The share of an asset's value or cost a lender will fund. For compute clusters, 70% to 80% of the bill of materials, against a contract.
A bond repaid from the cash flows and resale value of a pool of assets such as cars, aircraft, or equipment. Needs an independent estimate of what the assets will fetch.
0.01 percentage point; 100 basis points equal 1 percentage point.
The risk that a hedge's reference index moves differently from the exposure being hedged; for compute, the gap between an H100 index and the operator's actual mix of hardware, region, and commitment.
A contract that pays a fixed amount if an event occurs and nothing otherwise; its price approximates the market's probability of the event.
Tradable debt promise to pay interest and repay principal.
Short-term capital advanced against a signed contract and repaid when the cluster is delivered and the permanent loan funds.
Actual movement of cash during a period.
Buying a commodity, storing it, and selling it forward; the arbitrage that ties futures to spot. Unavailable for compute and electricity because neither can be stored.
An institution that becomes the counterparty to both sides of every contract, collects margin, values positions daily, and manages defaults through a fixed loss sequence.
Asset or contractual support pledged to reduce lender loss.
Exchange-traded contracts settling on a GPU rental index (CME/Silicon Data, ICE/Ornn, Architect). Let a builder sell rental revenue forward and a lender accept a cleared hedge.

A published reference price for GPU rental, built from posted asks, one venue's trades, or surveyed private transactions (Silicon Data, Ornn, Compute Desk). The construction determines what it measures.
Borrowing supported by the issuing company's overall balance sheet and cash flows.
Contractual interest payment on a bond.

In oil, the difference between refined product prices and crude. Here, the inference crack spread: token price minus the GPU-hour cost of producing the token. Contains real refining (software), margin, subsidy, and extraction.

Insurance on a borrower's debt: the buyer pays an annual premium in basis points and is made whole if the borrower defaults. The standard five-year spread is the cleanest public price of a company's credit risk.
Yield premium over a benchmark for default, liquidity, and related risk.
Discounted cash flow: present valuation of expected future cash flows.
Scheduled interest and principal payments.
The agreed order in which losses from a default are absorbed: the defaulter's margin, shared funds, the clearinghouse's capital, then other members.
A loan committed up front and drawn in stages; in GPU financing, as hardware is delivered against a specific customer contract.
Cash available for debt service divided by required debt service.
Sensitivity of a fixed-income asset's price to yield changes; also a timing concept.
Residual ownership claim that absorbs losses before debt.
A facility that lets a futures position be exchanged for delivery of the physical commodity, here delivered GPU capacity through a clearing platform.
Lease that economically finances use of an asset and is accounted for accordingly.
Today's prices for delivery at each future date. For a non-storable good it is an expectation plus a risk premium, not spot plus storage cost.
One accelerator rented for one hour; the spot unit of the compute rental market. Meaningful only with configuration, region, tenancy, and commitment attached.
The waiting list to connect new generation or load to the grid. Its length, in years, is the price of grid access that no market quotes directly.
Earnings or cash flow divided by interest expense.
Use or amount of debt relative to cash flow, assets, or equity.
Ability to meet obligations or transact without large price disruption.
Loan amount divided by the value of the collateral. Requires a value for the collateral, which is what compute hardware lacks.
Collateral posted against a position, sized to the move the price could make before the position can be liquidated.
Revaluing a position every day at the current market price.
Date when debt principal is due.
Replacing one party to a contract with another so the contract survives. The mechanism by which a clearinghouse steps in, or a defaulted lease moves to a new customer.
The customer that commits to take and pay for a project's output; in compute, the party signing the capacity contract.
Right to use an asset with lease expense and a recognized lease obligation under modern rules.
A derivative with no expiry that tracks spot through periodic funding payments between longs and shorts; originated in crypto markets and now offered on compute offshore.
Cash paid by a compute customer at signing, typically 20% to 50% of total contract value. It stands in for the customer's missing credit rating and funds the operator's equity in the cluster.
A price at which a trade actually happened, as opposed to a quote or a model value.
Financing primarily repaid from a project's assets and contracted cash flows.
The date a cluster is delivered, tested, and usable; payments and the contract term usually start here.
The share of a defaulted debt that creditors eventually get back. Dividing a CDS spread by one minus the recovery rate gives a rough annual default probability.
Replacing maturing or existing debt with new borrowing.
What an asset is worth at the end of the period over which it was financed. For accelerators, lenders assume zero because there is no liquid resale market to defend another number.
Benchmark return with minimal default risk, often proxied by sovereign debt.
Lending repaid from the sale of the thing financed; possible when the collateral has a reliable market price.
Secured Overnight Financing Rate: the overnight dollar rate, published by the New York Fed, over which loans are priced as a spread.
Special-purpose vehicle legally organized around a specific asset or transaction.
A lender's or third party's contractual right to take over a contract when a party fails to perform.
A set of binary contracts on the same quantity at successive strikes. Read together they give the market's probability distribution, and their area gives the expected value.
Contract requiring payment for committed capacity even if underused.
The length of a contract.
The price of the same capacity as a function of contract length, starting now. Not a forward curve: a three-year price is roughly the average of the forward prices inside it.
The excess of short-term over long-term rental prices. In compute it is large and reflects who has the credit to sign long contracts.
Compensation investors demand for holding longer-duration rate risk.
Price per GPU-hour times accelerators times hours over the whole term of a capacity contract. A multi-year number: compare it only with multi-year revenue.
What an asset fetches when sold. The number a lender needs after a default, and the one only a market can supply.
What an asset is worth to an owner who keeps operating it; computed from expected cash flows. Contrast value in exchange.
Return implied by a debt instrument's price and cash flows.
Reduction or repricing of other investment as one borrower absorbs saving or real resources.
Government debt stock divided by annual national output.
Failure to make promised debt payment or a coercive restructuring.
Government spending minus revenue during a period.
Debt payable in a currency the borrower does not issue.
Interest rate before subtracting inflation.
Government revenue minus non-interest spending.
Difference between effective interest rate and economic growth rate in debt dynamics.
Nominal interest rate adjusted for expected or realized inflation.
Risk that maturing debt cannot be refinanced on acceptable terms.
Debt issued or guaranteed by a national government.
High-density integration of compute, memory, and chiplets in one package.
Smaller die combined with others to create a larger system.
Extremely controlled manufacturing environment with very low particles.
TSMC family of chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging technologies.
Individual integrated circuit cut from a fabricated wafer.
Dynamic random-access memory used for working data.
Deep ultraviolet lithography used across many chip layers.
Electronic design automation software used to design and verify chips.
Extreme ultraviolet lithography using 13.5 nm light for critical advanced layers.
Semiconductor fabrication facility.
Business model that designs chips but outsources fabrication.
Manufacturer that fabricates chips designed by customers.
High Bandwidth Memory: stacked DRAM close to the accelerator.
High-density connection layer linking dies and memory in advanced packages.
Pattern used by lithography to define a chip layer.
Named process technology family such as N3 or N5, not one literal dimension.
Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test provider.
Layer connecting the semiconductor package to the circuit board.
Process design kit containing foundry rules and device models.
Completion and release of chip design data for mask and manufacturing preparation.
Vertical electrical connection passing through a silicon die, used in stacks.
Polished silicon disk on which many dies are fabricated together.
Fab capacity measure counting wafers entering a process each month.
Fraction of potential output that meets functional and performance requirements.
Contested label for broadly capable general-purpose artificial intelligence.
Capacity bought long-term against forecast steady demand, as a power purchase agreement is; the bottom layer of a procurement book.
A firm that leases long-term compute and sells it in shorter strips, earning the tenor premium; the compute analogue of a commodity trader.
Updating a system from new data or tasks while retaining prior capability.
The set of customers and contract terms a lender will finance. Compute is sold inside a three-year credit box.
Falling average cost or improving advantage as output or deployment grows.
All capacity already deployed and operating.

Hayek's observation that the facts needed to allocate resources are dispersed and cannot be centralized, so a price system is required to communicate them. A missing or false price is a failure of the system.
The next or newly available unit whose allocation and value drive decisions.
A cloud provider built around renting GPU capacity rather than a broad service catalogue; typically financed with project debt against customer commitments.

The process by which a market arrives at a price through the interaction of buyers and sellers with different private knowledge. Hayek: prices communicate dispersed knowledge that no central planner could collect.
Recursive self-improvement: AI materially accelerates development of successor AI systems.
Economic surplus earned because a hard-to-replace input is limited.
Something whose buyers will pay almost any price not to fall behind, so that it is allocated by bilateral contract and credit, not by an open market.
Hypothesized pace at which advanced AI capabilities increase.
The mechanism by which a shock in one market becomes a price change in another, with a characteristic lag. Each edge of the dashboard's linkage map is one.
Quality-adjusted computational work actually delivered to the target workload.
Share of created economic value retained by an actor through prices and margins.
Combining multiple supply-chain stages under coordinated control.

A cryptographic statement, produced by a trusted execution environment such as an NVIDIA confidential-computing enclave, that a computation ran as claimed. The strong fix for unverifiable cache counts, at a cost in speed and hardware eligibility.
Renting whole physical servers without a virtualization layer; the form open-weight inference prefers and small operators can offer.
A cheaper way to buy tokens in exchange for delayed delivery. Deferrable demand is the nearest thing compute has to storage.
The expected price per input token given a cache-hit rate h: h times the cached price plus (1 − h) times the input price. Ranking on it makes cache-dropping self-defeating.
Serving a request from a warm cache while reporting zero cached tokens, so the whole prefix is billed at the input price. Undetectable from the API response alone.
An input token whose key-value state was already in the provider's cache from an earlier request, so no prefill work was needed. Priced far below the input token, and not verifiable by the buyer.
A request sequence of known cache structure sent by a router or auditor to measure whether a provider's reported cache counts match reality.
An inference provider that quotes exactly the model builder's price and never moves, buying leaderboard presence rather than routed share.
The exponent r in a Tullock contest. At r = 2, halving your price quadruples your expected share: super-linear competition.
The sequential generation of output tokens, each of which reads the full KV cache. Limited by memory bandwidth, which is why HBM bandwidth sets inference throughput.
Training a smaller model to reproduce the outputs of a larger one. A decentralizing force: capability spreads faster than training compute.

Software that manages a user's data, context, and state and decides what is sent to a model: a chat app, a coding agent, an autonomous agent. Paid by users directly and sometimes by routers for order flow.
A provider's ability to produce the same tokens on different hardware, by analogy with a refinery's Nelson complexity index. Buys the option to rent out the scarce chip and serve on another.
The operator that owns or rents compute, loads a model's weights, and executes requests. Competes on hardware, kernels, electricity, and, when unobserved, on billing.
A token in the prompt sent to the model. Processed in the compute-bound prefill phase; priced per million.
The per-layer key and value vectors stored for every token in the context, held in accelerator memory so decode does not recompute them. Its size scales with context length.

Maximal extractable value: value that whoever orders transactions in a blockchain block can extract from the users being ordered. The router-provider relationship has the ordering without the validity check that MEV markets added.
The organization that trains and distributes a model. For open weights, it bears the training CapEx and can earn it back only by serving the model itself or by licensing.
Statistical tests that detect whether a provider is serving a different or degraded (for example, quantized) version of the model it claims to serve.
A model whose trained parameters are published for download, so that anyone with hardware can serve it. Distinct from open source, which would also publish training data and code.
The stream of requests a harness controls. Routers may pay harnesses for it, as brokerages are paid for routing retail stock orders.
A token generated by the model. Produced one at a time in the memory-bandwidth-bound decode phase; usually priced several times the input token.
The parallel pass over the whole prompt that computes attention state for every input token. Large matrix multiplications; compute-bound.
Reusing the KV cache of a shared prompt prefix across requests, so only the new tokens are prefilled. Implemented in serving engines such as vLLM and SGLang; sold as prompt caching.
The blockchain design that separates the party choosing a block's contents from the party proposing it, mediated by a relay that verifies validity. The analogue the souq lacks is the relay.
Delivering lower quality than promised where the buyer can learn it only statistically; the term is from online advertising, where verification firms and reputation scores were the response.
Storing weights and activations at lower numerical precision to cut memory and bandwidth needs. Raises throughput and can lower quality; a provider may do it without disclosure.
An inference provider that offers a static discount below the model builder's price.
An inference provider that updates prices frequently and undercuts deeply, sometimes to a tenth of the builder's price, to win the super-linear share the routing rule hands to the cheapest.
A service that maps a task from a harness to a model and an inference provider, charging a fee on routed tokens. OpenRouter is the canonical example.
Keeping a multi-request session on the provider that holds its cache. Per-request routing destroys it; the expected cost multiple rises with the number of providers.
An add-on price that is not salient and therefore not competed on, so competition on the headline price does not discipline it (Gabaix and Laibson). Cached-token pricing is the AI instance.
Token revenue per GPU-hour less the cost of the GPU-hour; the practitioner's name for the inference crack spread.
Using a small draft model to propose several tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, raising decode throughput without changing the output distribution.
Posting orders one intends to cancel to move a price. The financial-market analogue of quoting a token price one does not intend to honour on the cached leg.

A market structure in which independent stalls (harnesses, routers, model builders, inference providers) sell components of one product and the customer rarely deals with the maker directly. Coined by Tarun Chitra for open-weight model markets.
Different token prices at different hours, as in electricity tariffs; now visible in some providers' public listings.
An inference provider viewed as a refinery: it buys GPU-hours of various grades and sells a slate of token products.
Hardware-isolated execution whose state cannot be read or altered by the host operating system, and which can attest to what it ran. TEE for short.

A model of competition in which each participant's probability of winning equals its effort raised to a decisiveness exponent r, divided by the sum over all participants. OpenRouter's default routing is a Tullock contest in cheapness with r = 2.
